newsitem.title: FRANCE: French minister to stay away from Orient House.
newsitem.headline: French minister to stay away from Orient House.

text.p: French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette will skip a visit to controversial Palestinian offices at Orient House when he visits Jerusalem on Wednesday, his office said on Monday.
"As this is a working visit rather than an official visit, there are no plans for the minister to visit Orient House," ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told reporters.

Israel, which claims all Jerusalem as its own, campaigns to prevent foreign visitors from meeting Palestinian officials at Orient House in East Jerusalem. It says foreign visitors should meet Palestinians in self-ruled areas such as Gaza where Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has his offices.
De Charette set out for Israel on Monday afternoon on the first leg of a three-day Mideast trip which will also take him to Syria and Lebanon.

De Charette angered Israeli officials last year by announcing plans to visit Orient House while accompanying President Jacques Chirac on an earlier trip to Israel. He ended up cancelling his own visit to israel altogether.

The French foreign minister will hold talks with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Foreign Minister David Levy, President Ezer Weizman and former prime minister Shimon Peres before leaving Israel for Syria on Wednesday, Rummelhardt said.

He will also confer with Palestinian officials at a luncheon to be held at the French consulate general and at a meeting to be held at a university in Arab East Jerusalem, the ministry spokesman said.
The goal of de Charette's visit is to help get the peace process rolling once again despite rising tensions over Israeli plans to build new housing in the occupied West Bank.
"While there is no French plan, we are at the start of a new political phase (in the peace process) following the Hebron accord," Rummelhardt said.

"Our goals are try to restore confidence between the parties, search for common ground and help eliminate obstacles to resumed negotiations on the Palestinian and particularly on the Syrian aspects of the talks which must get off the ground sooner or later.
France has been pressing hard for a higher profile for itself and its European partners in Middle East diplomacy, now dominated by the United States.
But the ministry stressed its efforts were intended to complement Washington's efforts rather than compete with them.
A diplomatic shuttle by Chirac in October prompted grumblings from Washington that Paris was trying to compete with it during a delicate stage in the peace talks.

Israeli officials also privately complained about the trip, saying Chirac had demonstrated Paris' bias in favour of Arab states by publicly arguing with Israeli security guards in Jerusalem's Old City and repeatedly called for a Palestinian state, a policy opposed by the hard-line Netanyahu.

Israel last week lodged an official complaint after Paris disclosed that de Charette would spend just 24 hours in the Jewish state. Israeli Foreign Ministry spokesman Ygal Palmor said Paris had originally planned "a full state visit of two or three days".
The final schedule showed de Charette would spend two nights in Israel.
